summary: Defines the Extended Report (XR) packet type for RTCP, the control companion to RTP media streams. XR packets carry report blocks, with seven block types defined here, that convey statistics beyond the basic sender and receiver reports. This helps uses such as voice over IP monitoring. It also describes signaling XR use with SDP.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3611 adds Extended Report packets to RTCP so participants can report more detail about packet delivery and call quality. Applications can signal which report blocks they want to use.

subtitle: Extended RTCP reports for packet delivery, round-trip time, and voice quality.

tldr.problem: Standard RTCP sender and receiver reports contain limited statistics, while monitoring applications need more detail about packet delivery, delay, and voice quality.
tldr.mechanism: An Extended Report (XR) packet holds typed report blocks. The RFC defines seven block types and an SDP attribute for signaling which blocks participants should send.
tldr.outcome: XR supplements existing RTCP reports and does not change how the reporting interval is calculated. Its block and signaling registries allow later extensions.

today: RFC 3611 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2003. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Extended Reports Exist
sections.content:
RTP sessions use RTCP to exchange reception statistics. RFC 3611 defines an Extended Report (XR) packet for information that is useful across RTP profiles and does not fit in the existing sender or receiver report blocks.

The RFC defines seven report block formats: packet loss, duplicates, receipt times, reference times, delays, summary statistics, and VoIP metrics. XR packets can be combined with other RTCP packets and count as RTCP for bandwidth calculations.
sections.plainLanguage: XR adds more detailed reports to RTCP without changing its existing report types. The block formats cover packet delivery, timing, summary statistics, and voice-call metrics.

sections.title: XR Packet and Report Blocks
sections.content:
An XR packet has a two-word header followed by zero or more report blocks. Packet type 207 identifies XR. The packet length lets a receiver that does not recognize XR skip over the packet.

Each report block begins with a block type and a length. The receiver uses these fields to identify a block and find the next one, including when it does not understand a block type. Unknown or irrelevant blocks should be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet header identifies XR and gives its total length. Each block identifies its type and length, so a receiver can skip blocks it does not understand.

sections.title: Packet Loss, Duplicates and Receipt Times
sections.content:
Loss RLE and Duplicate RLE blocks describe receipt events by RTP sequence number using 16-bit run-length or bit-vector chunks. A run-length chunk represents 1 through 16,383 matching events; a bit vector represents 15 events. A null chunk can pad a block to a 32-bit boundary.

Thinning reduces the number of sequence numbers reported. Its value ranges from 0 to 15; at 0 every sequence number is included, while higher values report fewer. A Packet Receipt Times block reports timestamps for packets that arrived.
sections.plainLanguage: Packet-by-packet blocks report which sequence numbers arrived, were lost, or were duplicated. Run-length encoding compresses repeated results, and thinning reduces the number of results sent.

sections.title: Reference Time and Summary Statistics
sections.content:
A Receiver Reference Time block carries a receiver's NTP timestamp. A DLRR response reports how long elapsed after receiving that timestamp. The original receiver can subtract the timestamp and reported delay from its recorded arrival time to estimate round-trip propagation time.

The Statistics Summary block can report loss, duplicates, jitter, and IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit values over a sequence-number range. Flags identify which values are present; fields for unreported values are set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Reference-time blocks let participants estimate round-trip delay even when the receiver is not an RTP sender. Summary blocks report selected loss, duplicate, jitter, and hop-limit statistics.

sections.title: VoIP Call Metrics
sections.content:
The VoIP Metrics block reports packet loss separately from packets discarded by the receiver's jitter buffer. It also includes burst and gap measurements, delay, signal and noise levels, echo information, call-quality scores, and jitter-buffer settings.

The block is intended for voice applications using RTP and RTCP. Implementations must provide every defined field, using its specified unknown or default value when a measurement is unavailable. Conversational quality scores are not defined for multicast conferencing.
sections.plainLanguage: The VoIP block reports network loss separately from packets the receiver discards. It also summarizes delay, signal conditions, and quality measures when they are available.

sections.title: Signaling with SDP
sections.content:
XR blocks may be sent without prior signaling. For sessions configured in advance, the RFC defines the SDP attribute rtcp-xr at either the session or media level; a media-level value replaces the session-level value for that media.

The attribute names unilateral reports, such as packet loss and VoIP metrics, and collaborative reports such as round-trip-time measurement. When the attribute is present, participants should not send blocks that were not indicated. Size limits can be signaled for packet-by-packet blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: SDP can identify which XR blocks participants should send for a session. The signaling also helps limit block sizes and coordinate reports that require responses from another participant.

sections.title: Confidentiality and Bandwidth
sections.content:
XR can disclose more than standard RTCP reports. Packet-level reports can reveal multicast topology, loss rates, and delays, while VoIP metrics expose call-quality information. The RFC defines no new confidentiality mechanism.

Encryption can protect reports from eavesdroppers but also prevents third parties, such as service providers, from monitoring them. Large report blocks can lengthen RTCP reporting intervals, so applications should limit their size; thinning can help.
sections.plainLanguage: Detailed reports can reveal network and call information to people who observe them. Large reports can also reduce how often RTCP participants report, so applications should set size limits.
